claims.text: Slow cooling from the melt provides sufficient time for Mg diffusion and segregation to form Mg-rich intermetallic phases.
Mg-rich intermetallic phases act as preferential oxide-nucleation sites.
Intermetallic phases alter local electrochemical behavior in Mg-containing alloys.
Slow cooling transforms a metastable homogeneous solid solution into a precipitate-rich microstructure.
The slow-cooling-induced transformation improves high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The slow-cooling-induced transformation changes corrosion kinetics relative to rapid quenching.
The initial as-cast AlMgₓTiSnZn alloy is a homogeneous non-equilibrium solid solution with uniformly distributed elements.
The controlled comparison uses identically composed alloys subjected to rapid water quenching or slow furnace cooling.
The compared alloys are constrained to have density below 6 g/cm³.
Slow cooling preferentially produces Mg-rich intermetallic phases along grain boundaries.
Rapid water quenching retains a metastable single-phase microstructure.
Rapid quenching from a melt can substantially modify the resulting microstructure.
Intermetallic phases can influence micro-galvanic interactions during corrosion.
Intermetallic morphology, size, and spatial distribution can determine whether corrosion is impeded or localized corrosion is accelerated.
Mg-rich intermetallics promote a more adherent and uniform oxide scale during high-temperature exposure.
Slow-cooled specimens will have a higher volume fraction of Mg-rich intermetallics than rapidly quenched specimens.
Slow-cooled specimens will form denser and more protective oxide films and exhibit slower TGA weight gain.
Slow-cooled specimens will exhibit lower corrosion current densities than rapidly quenched specimens.
An inert or air-free cooling atmosphere prevents extraneous oxidation during cooling.
A lack of a statistically significant intermetallic increase or associated oxidation and corrosion differences would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The prediction specifically requires improved oxidation resistance and lower corrosion current, whereas the falsification rule can be read as accepting any systematic performance difference. A systematic worsening would contradict the directional prediction but might not trigger rejection under that wording.
